#### About Augustine of Hippo

Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was the North African bishop and theologian who shaped Latin Christianity’s doctrines of grace, sin, and the two cities. A former Manichaean and rhetor, he converted under Ambrose’s influence at Milan and narrated his restless heart in the Confessions.

### Interpretation

Augustine's sentence is a summary of his teaching on love rather than a quotation of a single text, and it is his most easily abused line. His point depends on a prior claim: love is a direction of the whole person, so where love is rightly ordered, the actions that follow are already governed. He is not licensing whatever one feels like — in his usage love has an object and an order, and most of his ethical writing is about correcting the order. Read without that framework the sentence means the opposite of what he meant.

#### Why it matters

The useful reading is diagnostic: look at what your actions are already serving. On this account conduct is not the puzzle; what you love is.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Love, and do what you will.”?

“Love, and do what you will.” comes from Sermons / Letters, (traditional form), attributed to Augustine of Hippo.

#### What does Augustine of Hippo mean by love?

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, freedom.
